title: Persona talktracks and GTM brief — ML / Backend / Platform teams
content:
Purpose:
This is a working GTM brief and talk-track playbook for three distinct engineering buyer personas: ML engineers, backend engineers, and platform teams. Use this when prepping SDR/AE outreach, demo scripts, and product marketing copy. Intention is practical: one-pagers for each persona + quick objection handlers + competitive framing.

Status notes (why this exists):
- We see different triggers by persona; messaging must map to technical levers (latency, cost, routing, observability) rather than generic product features.
- This doc is intentionally tactical and punchy — leave the deep technical benchmarks to the Serving Runtime team docs.
- Open questions at bottom for stakeholder input (SRE metrics, recent benchmark artifacts).

High level positioning we want to convey to all personas:
- Redwood is a production-first inference platform that unifies hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Core promises: predictable latency, measurable unit economics, and seamless rollout controls across environments.
- Differentiator: developer ergonomics + operational controls (canaries, automatic fallback, per-route cost telemetry) that map directly to engineers' success metrics.

Persona 1: ML Engineers
One-liner: Make model-serving 10x less guesswork — less tuning, more reliable predictions in production.
Top pain points:
- Models that perform well in eval but regress in production due to different prompt distributions and latency constraints.
- Cost blowups when trying to scale experiments or run A/Bs.
- Lack of observability into token-level costs and quality regressions.
Buying triggers:
- Need to ship a model to production with an SLO (latency or throughput).
- Evaluations reveal brittle behavior across datasets or prompt types.
- Security/compliance need pushes team off simple hosted options.
Technical evaluation checklist (what ML engineers ask for):
- End-to-end latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) for our sequence lengths.
- Model variant fallbacks and expected output drift when quantized.
- Tooling for prompt/eval sets and regression alerts.
- Support for KV cache/prefix caching and multi-shot contexts.
Talk tracks and demo focus:
- Show a live prompt-level quality dashboard + regression alert on an eval set — "see how a small model update changed rouge/accuracy and trigger canary rollback automatically".
- Emphasize batching/caching suggestions from Redwood Optimize and how those translate to immediate cost savings.
- Code snippet: integrate with the SDK, pin model version, and enable canary in <10 lines.
Objection handling (ML):
- "We host ourselves": ask about maintenance overhead, kernel/optimization upgrades, and benchmarks across GPU families. Offer side-by-side cost/latency estimate.
- "Loss in quality when quantizing": show curated quantization profiles for similar model families and explain fallback policy behavior.

Persona 2: Backend Engineers
One-liner: Ship dependable LLM endpoints that behave like any other backend service (SLOs, tracing, retries).
Top pain points:
- Unpredictable latency and cascading timeouts in user-facing flows.
- Integrating LLM calls into existing retry/circuit-breaker infrastructure.
- Nursing cost surprises from heavy tail usage.
Buying triggers:
- Product feature with user-visible latency requirements (chat, search ranking).
- Need for an SLA-backed endpoint or capacity commitment.
Technical evaluation checklist (backend):
- Per-request latency budget controls and circuit-breaker integrations.
- Streaming vs non-streaming behavior and connection semantics.
- Observability: traces, per-route token cost, and request-level metadata for debugging.
Talk tracks and demo focus:
- Walk through setting a per-route latency SLO, attaching a tracing hook, and simulating a downstream spike to show graceful fallback.
- Emphasize API parity: Redwood endpoints behave like REST services — status codes, idempotency keys, and deterministic retry semantics.
Example lines for outreach/email to backend lead:
- Subject: "Reduce user-visible LLM latency spikes by 3x — sample runbook"
- Body opener: "We helped an embedding-based search team cut p95 latency in half by adding prefix caching and a warm pool; can I show you a 10-minute demo?"
Objection handling (backend):
- "We need predictable billing": show per-route/prompt-level cost breakdown and reserved/dedicated capacity options.
- "We already use X cloud" (managed endpoints): frame Redwood as drop-in for teams that need better predictability, private network options, or lower unit cost at scale.

Persona 3: Platform Teams (Internal infra / SRE / platform engineering)
One-liner: Standardize inference across org with controls for security, cost accounting, and self-service.
Top pain points:
- Fragmented LLM usage across teams — lack of policy, cost visibility, or standardized deployment patterns.
- Difficulty reconciling cloud provider endpoints with on-prem/air-gapped workloads.
- Managing predictable capacity and SLAs for business-critical flows.
Buying triggers:
- Org-level mandate for data residency or new compliance requirement.
- Cost allocation headaches and need for chargeback with token-level visibility.
Technical evaluation checklist (platform):
- VPC/private deployment story, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs.
- Autoscale behavior, reserved pools, burst capacity semantics.
- Role-based access, policy controls, and per-team cost dashboards.
Talk tracks and demo focus:
- Show Console: per-team cost allocation, token-level chargebacks, and a sample policy to force dedicated capacity for PII-heavy routes.
- Emphasize migration path: start with Hosted API, then lift to Dedicated or Private with the same API surface.
Competitive framing notes for platform teams:
- Differentiate from CSP-managed endpoints: Redwood focuses on inference economics and cross-environment parity, not just hosting models.
- Versus open-source runtimes: lower operational burden and integrated rollout/tracing tools.

Competitive analysis bullets (short, for reps):
- Cloud AI providers: strong for general model access and global infra; weaker at cost transparency and per-route controls.
- Self-hosted runtimes (OSS): great control and no vendor lock-in; weak on developer ergonomics, managed fallbacks, and observability.
- Vertical inference vendors: may offer specialized optimizations but often lack unified hosted->private migration path and developer SDKs.
How we want reps to position (elevator 15–30s each):
- ML engineers: "Redwood helps you ship models without surprise regressions — monitoring + canaries + cost controls built-in."
- Backend engineers: "Think of your LLM as a first-class backend service with SLOs, tracing, and predictable fallbacks."
- Platform teams: "One API to govern inference across hosted, dedicated, and private — with chargeback, audit logs, and compliance-ready deployment patterns."

Demo checklist (for AE before show):
- 1-min setup: show model catalog and pin model version.
- 3-min: run a prompt against Hosted vs Dedicated variant and surface p95/p99.
- 3-min: enable a canary rollout and show automatic rollback on quality regression.
- 2-min: open Console cost dashboard, show per-route cost and team allocation.
- Wrap: ask for a production use case and next-step pilot criteria.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Get recent p95/p99 benchmark artifacts for Llama-2-like family from Serving Runtime (Jon).
- Add 2 short customer vignettes (ML-heavy startup, regulated enterprise) — ask CS for one-pagers.
- Validate quantization quality numbers for our recommended profiles.

Quick copy templates (short):
- Email subject lines: "Can we cut your LLM token costs by ~30%?", "Demo: treat LLMs like backend services (10 min)", "Pilot: private inference with audit logs"
- Demo ask: "If we run a 2-week pilot, what SLOs and dataset(s) should we use to evaluate?"

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep examples code-light for backend personas; ML personas want a snippet and eval hooks.
- Avoid deep marketing lingo in outreach — engineers prefer straight numbers and specific tradeoffs.
- Cross-reference: update this doc after each AE call with friction points and new objections.

End.
